posts.title: Body, gait or foot shape: which assessment do you need?
posts.summary: A practical guide to the different questions answered by X60, OneScan and F20.
posts.body:
Choosing an assessment system begins with a practical question: what do you want to help someone understand? A fitness coach may need a clearer starting point for a training conversation. A rehabilitation team may want a repeatable movement record. A footwear specialist may need a model that can continue into a fitting or design process. These are different workflows, even when the equipment appears to do a similar job.

The most useful demonstration connects the measurement, the report and the next step. Looking at all three makes it easier to judge whether a system belongs in your facility.

## Start with the conversation you need to have

Think about a typical appointment from the client's perspective. They arrive with a goal, take part in an assessment and leave with an explanation of what happens next. The equipment should support that explanation without making the session difficult to operate.

Body composition, posture and mobility can each contribute to that discussion. The [NEXBODY X60](/products/nexbody-x60) combines these assessment areas in a guided workstation workflow. When reviewing it, ask to see the instructions the person follows and how the operator moves between the different parts of the assessment. A polished screen is useful only when the people using it understand the process.

![NEXBODY X60 in a professional assessment setting](/media/products/x60/x60-clinical.png)

## Choose the measurement that fits the task

A system designed to describe foot shape answers a different question from one designed to analyse walking pressure. [F20](/products/f20-foot-scanner) captures the geometry of both feet for measurement and model-based workflows. [OneScan](/products/onescan-gait-analysis) records gait and plantar-pressure information on a dedicated platform. Where more than one assessment is needed, consider how the outputs will be reviewed together.

During a demonstration, look beyond a list of available measurements. Ask the supplier to show what each report contains, which outputs are included in the proposed configuration and what needs an additional service or integration. This creates a more reliable basis for comparing equipment.

## Read a report before deciding

Spend time with an example report. Consider whether the terminology suits the people who will explain it, whether the layout is readable and whether a follow-up comparison makes sense. Ask how a report can be shared, printed or exported in the configuration you are considering.

A report should help a qualified professional discuss the findings in context. It does not replace the judgement required for an individual's training, fitting or care. The operator's explanation remains part of the service.

## Plan for everyday use

The right choice also depends on your room, your team and your support arrangements. Review available space, operator training, language needs, data handling and the route for getting help. If another application will receive reports or models, test that transfer before relying on it.

A useful final step is to walk through one realistic appointment with the supplier. Follow the process from setup to explanation and export. The system that fits this complete workflow is more valuable than a feature list viewed on its own.

posts.title: Make repeat assessments easier to compare
posts.summary: Simple operational habits for more useful follow-up records.
posts.body:
A repeat assessment can help a professional explain what has changed and what needs more attention. Its value depends on more than the latest result. The way the appointment is prepared, carried out and recorded influences how useful the comparison will be.

For a facility introducing a new assessment service, consistency is an operating habit. It develops through clear instructions, staff training and records that explain the conditions around each appointment.

## Give each appointment a familiar structure

Begin with a shared process for preparing the equipment and guiding the person through the assessment. Use the product's instructions rather than relying on an operator's memory. Make sure the team knows which parts of the workflow are essential and where an exception should be recorded.

A consistent explanation can also make the experience easier for the client. Tell them what will happen, what they need to do and when the findings will be discussed. An assessment feels more useful when the person understands how it connects with their goals.

## Compare the process as well as the result

When reviewing two reports, consider whether the same assessment procedure was followed. Relevant differences in preparation, positioning or the way the appointment was run should be visible to the professional interpreting the records. A change in a measurement may require a conversation about those conditions before it becomes a conclusion about progress.

The [X60 assessment workflow](/products/nexbody-x60) brings posture, body composition and guided mobility assessment into one workstation. Facilities using several assessment areas should decide how they will explain each one and how the results will be brought together during the follow-up discussion.

![NEXBODY assessment report illustration](/media/products/x60/x60-analysis.png)

## Leave room for the person's wider context

Numbers and illustrations are most useful when considered alongside the person's goals, history and experience. A coach may ask how training has felt since the previous visit. A practitioner may need to consider findings from other assessments. The report provides information for that discussion; its appearance alone does not determine the next action.

Avoid presenting every difference as an improvement or a setback. Where the findings need clarification, explain the uncertainty and agree how the next appointment will be prepared. Qualified professionals should decide what the information means within their scope of practice.

## Make records usable for the whole team

Write notes in a way that another authorised colleague can understand. Record relevant exceptions and the explanation given to the client. Keep reports in the organisation's approved systems and confirm who can access them before introducing a new workflow.

Training should include report review and communication, as well as operating the equipment. A shared language helps staff describe the findings consistently without turning every appointment into the same conversation.

## End with an agreed next step

At the end of a follow-up, explain what the assessment adds to the wider plan. Agree whether another review is appropriate and what should remain consistent next time. This turns repeat testing into an ongoing professional service, rather than a collection of isolated reports.

A clear process does not remove every source of variation. It gives the team a better basis for recognising variation, explaining observations and deciding what to do next.

posts.title: Foot shape and plantar pressure tell different stories
posts.summary: Why 3D foot scanning and gait assessment can complement each other.
posts.body:
Foot shape and plantar pressure describe different aspects of an assessment. A three-dimensional model shows geometry. A pressure record shows contact with a sensing surface during the chosen task. Understanding this distinction helps footwear, orthotic and movement professionals select the right information for their workflow.

The two types of assessment can complement one another, but one should not be treated as a substitute for the other.

## A foot model describes geometry

A full-foot scan provides a digital representation that can be reviewed for measurements, left-right comparison or downstream model-based work. The [NEXBODY F20](/products/f20-foot-scanner) captures both feet together and supports full-foot measurements and STL model output.

For a footwear or orthotic workflow, the next question is how that output will be used. A team may need to review measurements, transfer a model to another application or retain a record for a later fitting. Confirm the receiving application's requirements and the outputs included in the proposed configuration.

![F20 full-foot scanning workflow](/media/products/f20/f20-workflow-2026.webp)

## A pressure record describes contact

A pressure-sensing platform records information about contact on its surface. A static assessment and a walking assessment are different tasks, so the instructions and the interpretation should match the purpose of the session.

[OneScan](/products/onescan-gait-analysis) supports gait and plantar-pressure assessment on a dedicated platform. Its reports address movement and contact information rather than producing the same output as a three-dimensional foot model. When evaluating the equipment, ask to see the assessment procedure and a report from the task your team expects to perform.

## Bring the information into one professional discussion

A practitioner may review foot geometry and pressure information while considering a fitting or movement question. That review still needs the person's history, the assessment conditions and the professional examination appropriate to the service being provided.

A model does not reveal all of the information present in a walking record, and a pressure illustration does not replace a detailed surface model. Keeping the role of each assessment clear makes the explanation easier for the person receiving it.

## Test the handover between systems

Before adopting a combined workflow, follow a real example through every stage. Check how files are named, how left and right feet are identified and what happens when a report or model is exported. Confirm that colleagues can find and interpret the records in the systems approved by your organisation.

If a model will be used for customisation, test the file in the actual receiving application. File format support is an important starting point, but a working transfer also depends on the measurement definitions and the steps used by the team.

## Choose equipment around the service

The most useful configuration is the one that supports a clear professional process. Start with the question you need to answer, choose the assessment that supplies the relevant information and agree how that information will be reviewed.

For some facilities, full-foot scanning is the immediate priority. Others may begin with gait and pressure assessment. Where both are required, planning the complete workflow helps the equipment contribute to a coherent service rather than two disconnected activities.

posts.body:
Body composition describes what your weight is made of, offering a more useful picture of health and fitness than a scale reading alone. The same scale number can reflect different amounts of muscle and fat in different people.

![Body composition assessment beyond body weight](/images/uploads/图片1.png "Body Composition")

Looking beyond the scale can help you make sense of changes in body weight during a fitness routine. It can also give you context for progress that a number alone might miss. This article explains what the measure includes, how common assessments work, and how to use results without treating them as a verdict.

**What Does Body Composition Measure?**

Body composition separates total weight into fat and fat-free components, including muscle, bone, organs, and water. Body fat percentage is the percentage of total body weight that is fat.

Two people with the same height and body weight can have different amounts of fat and muscle. **Body composition includes fat, protein, minerals, and body water, not just the number on a scale.** Those parts work together, but they do not all serve the same role.

![Body composition components including fat muscle and body water](/images/uploads/body-composition-analysis-infographic.png "Body composition components")

**Fat mass and its role**

Body fat is essential for normal body function. It stores energy, helps protect organs, supports hormone activity, and contributes to temperature regulation.

However, the amount and distribution of body fat can influence health. Fat stored around internal organs, known as visceral fat, is associated with certain metabolic and cardiovascular risks.

Body fat percentage is therefore useful information, but it should not be interpreted as a complete measure of health.

**Lean mass, muscle, bone, and water**

Fat-free mass includes everything in the body other than fat, such as muscle, bone, organs, and water.

Muscle mass is an important component because it supports movement, strength, and everyday physical activities. However, muscle mass and fat-free mass are not interchangeable terms.

Body water is another important factor. Normal changes in hydration can influence body composition estimates, particularly when using certain measurement technologies.

Understanding these components helps explain why body weight alone cannot describe changes in muscle and fat.

**How Is Body Composition Measured?**

A trained professional can estimate body composition with calipers, electrical impedance, imaging, air displacement, or underwater weighing. Each method uses different measurements, so results are most useful when you understand what the test estimates.

**No measurement gives a perfect account of every body component.** Technique, device type, and the conditions around a test can affect its accuracy and usefulness.

![Common body composition measurement methods](/images/uploads/图片2.png "Common body composition measurement methods")

**Skinfold calipers and BIA**

Skinfold calipers measure the thickness of folds of skin and nearby fat. A common assessment checks five sites: the abdomen, hip, arm, back, and thigh. With good technique, a skinfold estimate can be within plus or minus 3%.

Bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) sends a small electrical current through the body and uses the response to estimate body components. Readings typically take less than a minute. Hand-to-foot BIA measures the whole body and is more accurate than hand-to-hand or foot-to-foot devices.

Hydration can affect impedance and shift a BIA result. Keep conditions similar when comparing measurements, including hydration and the timing of each test.

**DEXA, air displacement, and underwater weighing**

DEXA uses low-level X-rays to estimate fat, lean tissue, and bone. Air displacement estimates body volume from how much air a person displaces in a sealed chamber. Underwater weighing estimates body density by comparing weight on land with weight underwater.

Before choosing a test, check these four practical details:

* Who performs the measurement or explains the result.
* Whether you can repeat the same method later.
* Whether the test fits your comfort and access needs.
* Whether the device has size limits that apply to you.

For progress checks, repeat the same method under similar conditions rather than comparing results from different devices.

**How Do Body Composition and BMI Differ?**

BMI uses height and weight to classify weight status, while body-composition measures estimate what that weight consists of. The key difference is that BMI does not separate fat from muscle.

**For adults, BMI equals weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared.** The categories are below 18.5, 18.5-24.9, 25.0-29.9, and 30.0 or above.

![Person reviewing a BMI chart and taking notes to assess body weight and health.](/images/uploads/图片3.png "BMI Chart and Body Weight Assessment")

Body mass index is a screening measure, not a direct measure of body fat. It can misclassify muscular people because muscle adds weight without showing how much of that weight is fat.

Body fat percentage estimates describe the share of total weight made up of fat. The ranges below vary by age group and sex, but they are estimates, not universal diagnostic cutoffs.

![Chart showing estimated body fat percentage ranges for women and men across age groups from 20–29 to 60 and older](/images/uploads/estimated-body-fat-percentage-ranges.png "Estimated Body Fat Percentage Ranges by Age and Sex")

A percentage outside one of these estimated ranges does not, by itself, diagnose a health problem. Testing methods also differ, so a result should be read with its method and limits in mind.

Age and sex can help frame an estimate, but neither tells you a person’s full health picture. A clinician may consider other information alongside BMI or a body fat percentage, such as medical history and how the person feels and functions.

Treat either measure as context for a broader health assessment, not as a stand-alone verdict.

![](/images/uploads/bmi-vs.-body-composition-explained.png "BMI vs. Body Composition: Key Differences Explained")

**Why Does Body Composition Matter for Health and Fitness?**

Body composition matters because both excess fat and too little muscle can affect health and the way everyday movement feels. How much and where fat is stored can add useful context, but no single measurement diagnoses a disease.

**Excess body fat is linked with heart disease, diabetes, and some cancers**. Visceral fat, stored around the organs, is one type of fat associated with health risks. These links describe risk, not a guarantee about any one person.

**Fat distribution and health risks**

Fat has ordinary functions, including energy storage and support for body processes. Its location matters because visceral fat around organs differs from fat stored just under the skin.

A body-fat reading cannot show the whole pattern on its own. Health history, daily function, and other clinical information help put a measurement into perspective.

**Muscle, movement, and performance**

Muscle supports movement and contributes to glucose metabolism. In daily life, muscle strength can make tasks such as carrying groceries or climbing stairs easier, though performance also depends on many other factors.

During exercise, fat serves as an energy source as activity continues beyond 20 minutes. It is a major contributor during endurance events lasting 30 minutes or more.

Very low body fat can also cause problems, including impaired immune function. In female athletes, low estrogen can contribute to bone loss, so lower is not always better.

No particular body type or percentage guarantees health or athletic performance. Focus on health, strength, and function rather than pursuing the lowest possible body-fat number.

**How Can You Improve and Track Body Composition?**

Sustainable body-composition change usually combines appropriate eating, regular movement, and enough recovery. Progress can involve fat loss, muscle gain, or both, and the scale may not show every change.

**Pair balanced meals and adequate protein with regular strength training and cardio.** Adults can aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity cardio or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity cardio weekly, plus strength training at least two days a week.

Pair nutrition with strength and cardio

Choose meals that support your energy needs and include protein to help maintain or build muscle. Resistance training gives muscles a reason to adapt, while cardio supports fitness and adds regular movement.

Recovery matters, too. A typical sleep target for adults is 7-9 hours per night, and enough rest can help you keep a routine going.

**Track trends, not single readings**

Use a plan you can follow, then look at measurements alongside changes in strength, energy, and daily function. These four actions can keep the process practical:

* Set a realistic goal that fits your needs.
* Combine resistance training with cardio.
* Support recovery by aiming for enough sleep.
* Compare repeat measurements made under consistent conditions.

  A single reading should never become the goal; choose a measure that helps you make a useful decision.

Scale weight can stay steady while muscle and fat change, so note more than one sign of progress. If a measurement would change a medical or weight-management decision, review it with a healthcare professional.

**FAQ**

**1. What is body composition analysis?**

Body composition analysis helps you understand what makes up your body weight, including body fat, muscle mass, body water, and other components. It provides a more detailed picture than body weight alone.

**2. Why is body composition more important than weight?**

Body weight only shows your total mass. Two people with the same weight may have different amounts of muscle and fat. Body composition analysis provides additional information to help professionals better understand physical condition and changes over time.

**3. What is a healthy body fat percentage?**

A healthy body fat percentage varies depending on factors such as age and sex. Rather than focusing on a single number, it is important to consider body fat alongside muscle mass, physical activity, and overall health.

**4. How often should you measure body composition?**

Measurement frequency depends on individual goals. For tracking fitness or wellness progress, regular assessments under consistent conditions can help identify meaningful trends over time.

**5. How accurate is body composition analysis?**

Accuracy depends on the measurement technology, testing conditions, and individual factors. Different methods estimate body components differently, so results should be interpreted in context rather than treated as exact measurements.

**Conclusion**

Understanding body composition is about more than tracking weight. By looking at body fat, muscle mass, and other key measurements, individuals and professionals can gain a clearer picture of physical condition and make more informed decisions.

For fitness centers, wellness facilities, and healthcare professionals, reliable body assessment tools can turn these insights into practical value.
